1 Peter 1.summary: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, writes to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ (1 Peter 1:1–2). Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for them, who are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation (1 Peter 1:3–5). They greatly rejoice, though now for a season they are in heaviness through manifold temptations, that the trial of their faith, much more precious than gold that perisheth, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ, whom having not seen they love (1 Peter 1:6–9). The prophets enquired and searched diligently of this salvation, searching what the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ and the glory that should follow (1 Peter 1:10–12). They are to gird up the loins of their mind, be sober, hope to the end, and as obedient children be holy in all manner of conversation, because it is written Be ye holy, for I am holy (1 Peter 1:13–17). They were redeemed not with corruptible things, silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot, foreordained before the foundation of the world (1 Peter 1:18–21). Seeing they have purified their souls in obeying the truth, they are to love one another with a pure heart fervently, being born again by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever, for the word of the Lord endureth for ever (1 Peter 1:22–25).
1 Peter 1.whereWeAre: 1 Peter follows James among the general letters. Peter writes to strangers scattered through the provinces of Asia Minor, blessing God for a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ, telling of the trial of their faith as gold tried with fire, and calling them to be holy and to love one another (1:1-25). Chapter 2 tells them who they are in Christ.

keyThemes.explanation: God hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance reserved in heaven (1:3-5).

keyThemes.explanation: The trial of their faith, much more precious than gold that perisheth, is found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ (1:6-9).

keyThemes.theme: Love for one another and the enduring word
keyThemes.explanation: They are to love one another with a pure heart fervently, being born again by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever (1:22-25).

1 Peter 2.summary: Laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings, the believers are as newborn babes to desire the sincere milk of the word, that they may grow thereby, if so be they have tasted that the Lord is gracious (1 Peter 2:1–3). Coming to Christ, a living stone, disallowed of men but chosen of God, precious, they as lively stones are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God by Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:4–5). He that believeth on the chief corner stone shall not be confounded, but to them which be disobedient the stone which the builders disallowed is made a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence (1 Peter 2:6–8). But they are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people, that they should shew forth the praises of him who hath called them out of darkness into his marvellous light, who in time past were not a people but are now the people of God (1 Peter 2:9–10). As strangers and pilgrims they are to abstain from fleshly lusts, have their conversation honest among the Gentiles, that they may by good works glorify God in the day of visitation (1 Peter 2:11–12). They are to submit to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake, whether to the king or to governors, as free but not using liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, honouring all men, loving the brotherhood, fearing God, and honouring the king (1 Peter 2:13–17). Servants are to be subject to their masters with all fear, not only to the good and gentle but also to the froward, for it is thankworthy if a man for conscience toward God endure grief, suffering wrongfully (1 Peter 2:18–20). Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth, who when he was reviled reviled not again, and who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, by whose stripes they were healed (1 Peter 2:21–24). They were as sheep going astray, but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of their souls (1 Peter 2:25).
1 Peter 2.whereWeAre: Chapter 1 ended with the word of the Lord that endureth for ever (1:25). Chapter 2 tells believers to desire the milk of the word, calls them lively stones, a chosen generation and a royal priesthood, and shows how strangers and servants should live and follow Christ's example (2:1-25). Chapter 3 turns to wives, husbands, and suffering for righteousness.

keyThemes.explanation: As newborn babes they are to desire the sincere milk of the word, that they may grow thereby (2:1-3).

keyThemes.explanation: They are to have their conversation honest among the Gentiles, that by good works the Gentiles may glorify God, and to submit to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake (2:11-17).

keyThemes.explanation: He his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, by whose stripes they were healed, and they are returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of their souls (2:21-25).

1 Peter 3.summary: Wives are to be in subjection to their own husbands, that if any obey not the word they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives, whose adorning is not outward plaiting of the hair and wearing of gold, but the hidden man of the heart, a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price, as Sara obeyed Abraham, calling him lord (1 Peter 3:1–6). Husbands are to dwell with their wives according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life, that their prayers be not hindered (1 Peter 3:7). All are to be of one mind, having compassion one of another, loving as brethren, pitiful, courteous, not rendering evil for evil, but contrariwise blessing, for the eyes of the Lord are over the righteous and his ears are open unto their prayers (1 Peter 3:8–12). Who is he that will harm them, if they be followers of that which is good, but if they suffer for righteousness' sake, happy are they, and they are to sanctify the Lord God in their hearts and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh a reason of the hope that is in them with meekness and fear (1 Peter 3:13–15). Having a good conscience, that they which falsely accuse their good conversation in Christ may be ashamed, for it is better to suffer for well doing than for evil doing (1 Peter 3:16–17). Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but quickened by the Spirit, by which he went and preached unto the spirits in prison, which sometime were disobedient in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein eight souls were saved by water (1 Peter 3:18–20). Baptism doth also now save us, the answer of a good conscience toward God, by the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who is gone into heaven and is on the right hand of God, angels and authorities and powers being made subject unto him (1 Peter 3:21–22).
1 Peter 3.whereWeAre: Chapter 2 ended with Christ the Shepherd and Bishop of their souls (2:25). Chapter 3 speaks to wives and husbands, calls all to be of one mind and to bless, tells them to be ready to give a reason of their hope, and shows Christ suffering for the unjust and now at God's right hand (3:1-22). Chapter 4 calls them to arm themselves with the same mind.

keyThemes.theme: Christ's suffering, vindication and rule
keyThemes.explanation: Christ hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, and is gone into heaven, angels and authorities and powers being made subject unto him (3:18-22).

1 Peter 4.summary: Forasmuch as Christ hath suffered for us in the flesh, the believers are to arm themselves with the same mind, for he that hath suffered in the flesh hath ceased from sin, that he no longer should live to the lusts of men but to the will of God (1 Peter 4:1–2). The time past may suffice to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when they walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries, wherein the Gentiles think it strange that they run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of them, who shall give account to him that is ready to judge the quick and the dead (1 Peter 4:3–6). The end of all things is at hand, so they are to be sober, watch unto prayer, have fervent charity among themselves, for charity shall cover the multitude of sins, and use hospitality one to another without grudging (1 Peter 4:7–9). As every man hath received the gift, he is to minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God, that God in all things may be glorified through Jesus Christ (1 Peter 4:10–11). They are not to think it strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try them, but rejoice inasmuch as they are partakers of Christ's sufferings, and if they are reproached for the name of Christ, happy are they, for the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon them (1 Peter 4:12–14). Let none of them suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an evildoer, or a busybody in other men's matters, yet if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but glorify God on this behalf (1 Peter 4:15–16). Judgment must begin at the house of God, and if first at us, what shall the end be of them that obey not the gospel of God, so let them that suffer according to the will of God commit the keeping of their souls to him in well doing, as unto a faithful Creator (1 Peter 4:17–19).
1 Peter 4.whereWeAre: Chapter 3 ended with Christ gone into heaven, angels and powers subject to him (3:22). Chapter 4 tells believers to live no longer to the lusts of men, to love and use hospitality, not to think the fiery trial strange, and to commit their souls to a faithful Creator (4:1-19). Chapter 5 gives instructions for elders and closes the letter.

keyThemes.explanation: The end of all things is at hand, so they are to be sober, have fervent charity, use hospitality, and minister their gifts as good stewards of the manifold grace of God (4:7-11).

keyThemes.theme: Suffering as sharing in Christ's sufferings

keyThemes.theme: Suffering for the right reasons

keyThemes.theme: God's judgment and trust in the faithful Creator
keyThemes.explanation: Judgment begins at the house of God, and those who suffer according to God's will are to commit the keeping of their souls to a faithful Creator (4:17-19).

1 Peter 5.summary: Peter, who is also an elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, exhorts the elders to feed the flock of God, taking the oversight not by constraint but willingly, not for filthy lucre but of a ready mind, neither as being lords over God's heritage but being ensamples to the flock (1 Peter 5:1–3). When the chief Shepherd shall appear, they shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away (1 Peter 5:4). The younger are to submit themselves unto the elder, and all are to be clothed with humility, for God resisteth the proud and giveth grace to the humble (1 Peter 5:5). They are to humble themselves under the mighty hand of God, casting all their care upon him, for he careth for them (1 Peter 5:6–7). They are to be sober and vigilant, because their adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about seeking whom he may devour, whom they are to resist stedfast in the faith, knowing that the same afflictions are accomplished in their brethren in the world (1 Peter 5:8–9). The God of all grace, who hath called us unto his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after that they have suffered a while, make them perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle them (1 Peter 5:10–11). Peter has written briefly by Silvanus, a faithful brother, exhorting and testifying that this is the true grace of God wherein they stand, and the church that is at Babylon and Marcus his son salute them, with peace to all that are in Christ Jesus (1 Peter 5:12–14).
1 Peter 5.whereWeAre: Chapter 4 ended with a call to commit the keeping of their souls to a faithful Creator in well doing (4:19). Chapter 5 tells elders to feed the flock, the younger to submit, all to cast their care on God and resist the devil, and closes with a prayer, greetings from Babylon, and peace (5:1-14). 2 Peter follows.
